newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Cenbank says global offer a limited success.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Cenbank says global offer a limited success.

text.p: Brazil's launch of a $750 million, five-year global bond on Monday was a limited success, Central Bank director Gustavo Franco said.
"We didn't score a hatful of goals, but we brought the trophy home," Franco told reporters, using the soccer terminology that dominates Brazilian conversation. "You have to celebrate even a 1-0 win."
Brazil's bond, its debut dollar global offering, traded at a spread of about 285/275 basis points over U.S. Treasuries in London on Thursday, compared with 265 at its launch.

Traders cited nervousness over the Mexican peso, which closed at over eight to the dollar for the first time on Wednesday, as contributing to Brazil's rising spread. A rally in U.S. Treasuries was also mentioned.

Franco said he and other officials had considered offering the bond at 230 points over Treasuries before spreads of emerging market debt began to climb in October on worries over Argentina, Mexico and Russia.

Even so, the 35-basis point hike on the Brazilian bond was less sharp than the widening of spreads seen in emerging debt as a whole during the month. "Our worsening was less than half the general decline," Franco said.
He also said the main aim of the launch -- to reduce the cost of future Brazilian debt issues and set a lower benchmark for perception of the country's risk -- had been acheived.

Franco denied that concerns over Brazil's trade deficit contributed to the less-than-euphoric reception of the bond. Markets were taken by surprise when Brazil posted a larger-than-expected $655 million deficit in September.

"The investors we targetted are first-time buyers who are going to hold on to this paper for five years," he said. "They think of a thousand things before investing and it's not one day's news that's going to change their minds."
When compared with similar debt issued by Argentina and Mexico, trading at spreads of 390 and 315 points over Treasuries respectively, Brazil's launch appeared "excellent," he said.

Franco said that between 55 and 65 percent of Brazil's global bonds had been purchased by investors who had never before held Brazilian debt, many of them unwilling to face the volatility of the Brady market.

About half of buyers were from Asia and the Middle East, roughly 20 percent from the United States and 20 percent from Europe, while Latin America and funds specialising in the region accounted for the rest, he said.
